title: Pooled climate weights gave no clear gain over a binary gate in six forward tests with observed weather
abstract: We tested whether a published partial climate weight improved on binary family decisions outside its five source weighting families. We rebuilt 14,312 series from six other families: US river flow, ice dates, Japan cherry dates, US bird counts, vegetation index and national dengue cases. All endpoint scores matched the published values to rounding precision. We fitted family weights with rolling forecasts in 1990-2004 and froze them for tests in 2005-2024 where present. With observed weather, the equal-family mean of median skills was 0.55394 for partial weights and 0.54990 for the gate. The gain was 0.00403. Its 95% location-only interval was 0.00010 to 0.00651, but a joint interval with shared year blocks and refitted weights was -0.00590 to 0.00644. Vegetation had the largest point gain, 0.02349, with a joint interval across zero. Family weights exceeded individual weights by 0.01071; the main joint interval was above zero, but a fixed-weight time resample crossed zero. The six-family evidence does not establish an advantage over binary family decisions. Limits include known source outcomes, six fixed families, revised records, conditional source preprocessing and observed rather than forecast weather. Code, source hashes, aggregate moments, full comparisons, checks and static figures are included. External record tables remain outside the bundle.
